listitem.simpara: Wrote guidance on storytelling in user stories.

chapter.simpara: Here is a classic user story:

blockquote.simpara: I, as a prospective contributor, want a vision document so that I can decide whether to join Papillon Journey.

chapter.simpara: Functional? Yes. Inspiring? Not quite. It captures the user’s need, but where is the story?
User stories emerged to humanise requirements, moving away from dry specs like:

blockquote.simpara: The project shall publish a vision document.

chapter.simpara: This I, as a (role), want (function) so that (business value) template Cohn 2004 was a leap forward, but it still falls short of true storytelling.

section.title: Stories are about change
section.simpara: According to Robert McKee’s bestseller Story McKee 1997, a story narrates a meaningful change in the life of a character — a change triggered by conflicts and experienced as a shift in value.

To ground storytelling in software engineering, we can draw from Strategyzer’s Value Proposition Canvas Osterwalder et al. 2014, where conflicts are the user’s pains, and the shift in value comes when features relieve those pains and unlock gains.
Stories follow a universal arc: context (the user’s job), conflict (their pains), confrontation (their efforts to overcome them, supported by what teams deliver), and resolution (their gains).
With this in mind, we can enhance the classic user story template:

blockquote.simpara: As a (role) trying to (job), but facing (pains), I want (feature), so that (gains).

section.simpara: We put it to work in ϛε1:

blockquote.simpara: As a prospective contributor evaluating whether to invest time in Papillon Journey, I prefer not having to guess the project’s purpose, goals, value propositions, and action plan by trawling through GitHub issues or discussions — as is often the case in open source. Instead, I want these elements articulated in a concise 2–4-page vision document, so that I can quickly decide whether the project aligns with my interests, contribute effectively, and share my enthusiasm for it.

section.simpara: This template does not just align with the essence of storytelling — transforming a negative into a positive — it also feeds directly into the Value Proposition Canvas. Win–win. That said, giving the I in the user story a backstory would engage teams even more.

section.title: Stories drive action
section.simpara: Meet Joséphine, our prospective contributor considering whether to join Papillon Journey. Imagine bringing her user story to life with a personal narrative ϛε1:

simpara.quote: Thank you so much for the redesign of our site. Customers keep telling us how intuitive, clean, and easy it is to navigate!

blockquote.simpara: The SMS notification lit up Joséphine’s phone, briefly breaking the quiet focus of her cosy home office — and it made her day. Messages like this are what keep her going. She is a freelance web designer and front-end developer who has helped several small businesses thrive online. Nothing makes her happier than seeing her clients reach their goals through the UX she has crafted, and watching their users genuinely enjoy the experience. Her growing portfolio of success stories attests to this.

Just before the SMS pulled her away, Joséphine had been immersed in the Papillon Journey GitHub project, scrolling through issues and discussions. The idea of repurposing JRPG mechanics for graduate-level education set her imagination racing with UX concepts, all promising serious design challenges — the kind that could stretch her skills, enrich her portfolio, and open doors to new opportunities. She wanted to contribute.

She set her phone on the desk and turned her eyes back to her laptop screen, picking up where she had left off. She had already spent an hour exploring the project, and her seasoned UX instincts were starting to raise red flags — questions piling up unanswered with every page she opened. Whose problems was Papillon Journey actually aiming to solve? Why opt for a JRPG format over a straightforward course catalogue? How was success meant to be gauged — through completion rates, skills gained, player retention, or something else? And, zooming out, what did the project’s roadmap look like, even loosely sketched, over the next three to five years?

She couldn’t find any document that brought these elements into one place. The fragments pieced together from various issues and comments fell short, leaving her uncertain if contributing would truly align with the project’s direction or meaningfully strengthen her professional trajectory. As a freelancer with limited time for open source, she couldn’t afford guesswork. She bookmarked the repo, gulped down her remaining coffee, and shifted to another important task — one backed by a clear path forward.

To boost the odds that Joséphine contributes on her next visit, a concise 2–4-page vision document answering these questions is essential. Walking her through her first contribution comes next — but that’s another story.

section.simpara: Does this not make you want to write that vision document? This narrative does not just humanise the user story: it inspires teams to deliver solutions that truly matter.

section.title: Does your story hold?
section.simpara: Before acting on a user story, reread it with a sceptic’s eye. While the feature is still on paper and the resolution still a hope, ask three questions:

listitem.simpara: Does the feature relieve each pain? Take them one by one. A pain the feature leaves untouched is a conflict the user story never resolves.
Does it unlock each gain? A gain does not come for free. It should be easy to see why the feature delivers it.

Does it shift value, turning each pain into one or more gains? Every pain must end up as a gain. The reverse is not required: a gain can stand on its own. If every gain merely mirrors a pain, the feature goes no further than putting things right; extra gains can give people another reason to choose one product over another.

blockquote.simpara: As a prospective contributor evaluating whether to invest time in Papillon Journey, I prefer not having to guess the project’s purpose, goals, value propositions, and action plan by trawling through GitHub issues or discussions — as is often the case in open source. Instead, I want these elements articulated in a concise 2–4-page vision document, so that I can quickly decide whether the project aligns with my interests, contribute effectively, and share my enthusiasm for it.

row.entry: Does the feature relieve each pain?
Pain: guessing the project’s purpose, goals, value propositions, and action plan
A document that articulates them leaves nothing to guess.
Pain: trawling through issues and discussions
Gain: quickly deciding whether the project fits her interests
A two-to-four-page document is concise enough for a quick read.
A vision document is not an onboarding guide, but it could show Joséphine where to find one.
A clear, compact vision is something she can point others to.
With nothing left to guess, she can decide quickly.
Without the hunt, the decision comes sooner.

section.simpara: When a check fails, do not dismiss it and call the user story finished. Pause and take another look:

listitem.simpara: Take it out. If the project still wants to address it, it is material for another user story. If that pain really drives the user story, the feature itself needs rethinking.
Your call. Drop it, or keep it as a reminder if the project cares about it and no other user story covers it yet. But make it clear somewhere that this user story is not expected to deliver it.

varlistentry.term: A pain is not turned into a gain.

listitem.simpara: Something is off. Perhaps the user story leaves the gain unstated; if so, write it down. If relieving this pain leads to no gain, rethink the feature or the pain it promises to address.

section.simpara: The checks reveal one unaddressed expectation in Joséphine’s story: contributing effectively needs its own user story. The vision document can focus on helping her decide whether to join.
Now pick a user story you wrote recently and put it through the three checks. Does it hold, or does it break?
